title: Classic Vinaigrette

items.raw: 1 small shallot, very finely minced (about 2 tablespoons)
9 tablespoons (½ cup plus 1 tablespoon) extra-virgin olive oil

steps.text: Put the minced shallot, vinegar, and salt in a small bowl or jar and let it sit 10 minutes. The vinegar softens the shallot’s raw bite and the salt dissolves completely — salt will not dissolve once the oil is in.
Whisk in the Dijon and the honey, if using. The mustard is what holds the dressing together; it coats the oil droplets and keeps them from separating.

Pour in the olive oil in a slow, thin stream while whisking constantly, until the dressing is glossy and slightly thickened. Or put everything in a jar, close the lid tightly, and shake hard for 20 seconds.
Add several grinds of pepper. Taste it on a leaf of lettuce, not off a spoon — on its own it should taste a little too sharp and a little too salty, because the greens will mute it.
Toss the salad with a few spoonfuls just before serving, adding more only if the leaves look dry. Leaves should glisten, not sit in a pool.

notes.label: The ratio
notes.text: three parts oil to one part vinegar is the starting point. With a mellow vinegar like sherry or champagne, you can go closer to two to one.

notes.label: Ahead of time
notes.text: keeps a week in a jar in the refrigerator. The olive oil will cloud and firm up when cold; let it sit out 15 minutes and shake again.

notes.label: Variations
notes.text: swap the vinegar for lemon juice; add a small grated garlic clove; stir in chopped chives, tarragon, or parsley just before using.

notes.label: Beyond salad
notes.text: spoon it over warm roasted vegetables, boiled potatoes, green beans, or grilled fish.

openQuestion: This is a best guess — a classic shallot and Dijon vinaigrette. Whose house dressing is this, and what goes on it? Tell me whether yours uses red wine vinegar, sherry vinegar, or lemon; shallot or garlic; and whether there is mustard or honey in it.
